info.bio: Influenciados por las melodías de los Beatles, las armonías vocales de los Beach Boys y la fortaleza instrumental de los Who, el grupo The Move resultó ser una de las formaciones más destacadas del Reino Unido en los últimos años de la década de los sesenta, derivando su importancia del talento atesorado por el genial compositor y multiinstrumentista Roy Wood, quien en sus composiciones tanto ahondaba en el pop o la psicodelia, como en el rock progresivo, el rock’n’roll o la música clásica.

scenes.name: Llega la psicodelia británica
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: En otoño de 1966 la palabra «psychedelic» llegó a Gran Bretaña: el Melody Maker la presentó el 22 de octubre como «el gran contraataque americano» y la prensa la aplicó a los Move, Creation, los Who y los californianos Misunderstood («vamos de viaje al subconsciente»): freak-outs, volumen y asalto sonoro. Fue el momento en que empezó el rock: virtuosismo, improvisación y ambición, aún contenidos en el single. Cream, tres veteranos del R&B, sacó «I Feel Free»; Jimi Hendrix, llegado en septiembre con Chas Chandler, era el negro americano empapado de soul, blues, Dylan y ácido que los británicos imitaban: «Hey Joe» y «Stone Free» («Free Feeling»). Donovan volvió con «Sunshine Superman». El 23 de diciembre abrió UFO en el Blarney Club, la primera noche del underground, con Pink Floyd en improvisaciones de diez minutos; en Nochevieja, Psychedelicamania en el Roundhouse con los Move, Pink Floyd y los Who. Los mods quedaban atrás.

podcast.body: MOVE, a Vancouver-based band, founded Network Records because they were unable to find any other label willing to release their music. "Network Records of Vancouver, a label founded by a band called MOVE when they couldn't find anyone to touch their stuff."

xref.title: Claim to Devil Horns (November 1974)
xref.body: Gene Simmons claimed to be the first to flash the "devil horns" gesture in November 1974. He attempted to trademark the move with the US Patent and Trademark Office on June 16, 2017, but withdrew the claim due to significant public backlash. "He even tried to trademark the move with the US patented trademark office on June 16, 2017."

xref.title: Major Label Signing (1988)
xref.body: By 1987, R.E.M. felt they had exhausted their potential as an indie band and faced a choice between a career stall or signing with a major label. They signed with Warner Brothers on April 8, 1988, receiving a $6 million check. Michael Stipe stated the move was necessary for "worldwide" distribution, as IRS's distribution capabilities had reached their limit. Peter Buck reflected on the band's ongoing struggle to balance artistic integrity with commercial moves, acknowledging they were "part of the machine." "So it came to pass on April 8, 1988, R.E.M. signed with Warner Brothers and took home a $6 million check."

xref.title: Balancing Art and Commerce
xref.body: Peter Buck articulated the band's struggle to balance artistic integrity with commercial interests, expressing their fear of diluting the band's essence while acknowledging their role within the music industry "machine." Michael Stipe further explained the move to Warner Brothers by stating that IRS's distribution capabilities had reached their limit, necessitating a partnership with a label capable of global reach. "In our own case, R.E.M. is always trying to figure out where the line is between commerce and what we do, because it means something to us."

xref.title: Contribution to Nu-Metal
xref.body: Despite controversies, Body Count persevered and played a significant role in the emergence of the nu-metal movement during the mid to late 1990s, influencing bands like KoRn, Slipknot, and Limp Bizkit. "But the band continued, and they were a big part of the move into new metal in the middle in late 90s. So basically, you can draw a line from Body Count, right through corn, slipknot, and limp biscuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ziggy Stardust - Breakthrough and Theatricality
xref.body: The creation of Ziggy Stardust brought Bowie out of almost a decade of obscurity, elevating rock's theatricality to new levels. The character was presented as a "doomed spaceman with a Messiah concept," potentially involved in populating Earth with "Japanese style kabuki actors." Bowie used Ziggy to explore fashion, utilize his professional mime training from the 1960s, and experiment with art and sexuality. "this was the move that brought Bowie out of obscurity after almost a decade of dead ends."
